args.summary: 23-year-old man with no prior illness, trauma or anticoagulant use. Two days ago he developed non-radiating interscapular pain, followed by progressive paraplegia (legs 0/5, arms 5/5), no perianal sensation and bowel/bladder incontinence. The bulbocavernosus reflex is preserved. MRI shows an epidural hematoma from C6 to T2 compressing the cord and the posterior thecal sac, with no traumatic or structural lesion described. Platelets are normal at 250,000/µL. WBC is 13,000/µL with 85% neutrophils, which is likely a stress response; he has no fever. PT/INR, aPTT and fibrinogen were not reported. Vital signs are described as stable. This is a neurosurgical emergency and needs urgent decompression.
working_diagnoses: Spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma C6-T2 with acute cord compression (severe cervicothoracic myelopathy/complete motor deficit)
Hematoma secondary to occult vascular malformation (epidural AVM/cavernous malformation)
Spinal epidural abscess with hemorrhagic component (less likely: afebrile)
next_actions: Emergent neurosurgical consultation and decompressive laminectomy with hematoma evacuation
Correct any coagulopathy found on pre-operative labs; keep NPO; hold all antithrombotics
Maintain MAP >85 mmHg for spinal cord perfusion; Foley catheter
Send hematoma for histopathology/culture to look for vascular malformation or infection
Admit to ICU after surgery for neuro checks

His legs are paralysed (0/5), he has no perianal sensation and he is incontinent of bowel and bladder (physical_exam_003, hpi_001). He has had emergency laminotomy with hematoma evacuation (procedure_result_009). He needs close neurological and blood-pressure monitoring after surgery, because the hematoma could come back and the cord needs adequate perfusion. The cause of the bleed is still unknown: he has no trauma or anticoagulant use (hpi_002), and platelets are normal (lab_005). PT/INR, aPTT and fibrinogen were ordered but not reported.
args.followup_or_handoff: Handoff to the neurosurgery/neuro-ICU team. (1) Do neurological exams every hour, including strength, sensory level and sphincter function. If he gets worse, repeat the MRI urgently and consider going back to theatre. (2) Keep MAP above 85 mmHg for 5–7 days to support cord perfusion. (3) Send PT/INR, aPTT and fibrinogen now, because they were never reported. If they are abnormal, work up a bleeding disorder, including factor levels and von Willebrand studies. Hold all anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs; use mechanical DVT prophylaxis only until neurosurgery approves heparin. (4) Follow up hematoma histopathology and culture. Consider spinal MRA or catheter angiography to look for an occult vascular malformation. Recheck WBC and temperature (WBC 13,000 with neutrophilia). (5) Place an indwelling bladder catheter and start a bowel regimen, pressure-injury prevention and early physical therapy and rehabilitation. (6) Arrange spinal cord injury rehabilitation and outpatient neurosurgery follow-up.
